leftEvidence.role: The mountain and those called blessed
leftEvidence.title: Teaching, healing, and crowds gather before the mountain

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus teaches in Galilee, announces the Kingdom, heals disease, and becomes known across a wide region.
points.right: Seeing the crowds, Jesus goes up the mountain, sits, and receives his disciples.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: People bring the afflicted, Jesus heals them, and multitudes from several regions follow.
points.right: He opens his mouth and teaches them.

compares.posture: The antecedent explains the large following; the opening narrows attention to disciples around the seated teacher.

rightEvidence.role: The mountain and those called blessed
rightEvidence.title: Jesus sits and begins to teach

compares.tension: The discourse’s immediate and wider audiences remain visible without an invented movement.
compares.title: Crowds gather and disciples draw near

leftEvidence.role: The mountain and those called blessed
leftEvidence.title: The poor in spirit receive the Kingdom

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus calls the poor in spirit blessed.
points.right: Jesus stands on a level place among disciples and a crowd, heals, and addresses the poor, hungry, weeping, and rejected.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The Kingdom of Heaven is said to be theirs in the present tense.
points.right: Four blessings are followed by four woes directed to the rich, full, laughing, and well-spoken-of.

compares.posture: Matthew and Luke open corresponding blessing sequences with materially different wording.

rightEvidence.title: Luke places blessings and woes on a level place

compares.tension: Matthew adds “in spirit”; Luke directly addresses the poor and later speaks woes to the rich.
compares.title: Poor in spirit and poor

leftEvidence.role: The mountain and those called blessed
leftEvidence.title: Those who mourn will be comforted

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus calls those who mourn blessed.
points.right: Jesus stands on a level place among disciples and a crowd, heals, and addresses the poor, hungry, weeping, and rejected.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Their present mourning is set beside future comfort.
points.right: Four blessings are followed by four woes directed to the rich, full, laughing, and well-spoken-of.

compares.posture: Both sayings hold present grief beside a promised reversal.

rightEvidence.title: Luke places blessings and woes on a level place

compares.tension: Matthew says mourners will be comforted; Luke says present weepers will laugh and follows with a woe to those laughing now.
compares.title: Mourning, weeping, comfort, and laughter

leftEvidence.role: The mountain and those called blessed
leftEvidence.title: The gentle will inherit the earth

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus calls the gentle blessed.
points.right: The psalm calls one person blessed for rejecting wicked counsel and delighting in the LORD’s law.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: They are promised inheritance of the earth.
points.right: Fruitful tree and driven chaff images end in known and perishing ways.

compares.posture: Matthew’s inheritance wording and Psalm 1’s two ways place present character beside future outcome.

rightEvidence.title: Blessing opens into two ways and two outcomes

compares.tension: The promised earth and the known way are related outcomes, not identical images.
compares.title: The gentle inherit and the righteous way endures

leftEvidence.role: The mountain and those called blessed
leftEvidence.title: Hunger for righteousness will be filled

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus calls those who hunger and thirst for righteousness blessed.
points.right: Jesus stands on a level place among disciples and a crowd, heals, and addresses the poor, hungry, weeping, and rejected.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Their desire is promised satisfaction.
points.right: Four blessings are followed by four woes directed to the rich, full, laughing, and well-spoken-of.

compares.posture: Both blessings promise filling to the hungry.

rightEvidence.title: Luke places blessings and woes on a level place

compares.tension: Matthew names righteousness as hunger’s object; Luke addresses those hungry now and gives a corresponding woe to the full.
compares.title: Hunger for righteousness and hunger now

leftEvidence.role: The mountain and those called blessed
leftEvidence.title: The merciful will receive mercy

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus calls the merciful blessed.
points.right: James prohibits partiality and says God chose the poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the Kingdom.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Their mercy toward others stands beside promised mercy for them.
points.right: Neighbor love is called royal law, the whole law’s integrity is stressed, and mercy triumphs over judgment.

compares.posture: Matthew’s reciprocal blessing and James’s judgment saying make mercy consequential.

rightEvidence.title: The poor, Kingdom, neighbor love, and mercy meet judgment

compares.tension: Neither source reduces mercy to sentiment, while their arguments and audiences differ.
compares.title: Mercy received and mercy at judgment

leftEvidence.role: The mountain and those called blessed
leftEvidence.title: The pure in heart will see God

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus calls the pure in heart blessed.
points.right: Jesus contrasts vulnerable earthly treasure with treasure in heaven.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: They are promised sight of God.
points.right: The heart is said to be where the treasure is.

compares.posture: Both sayings place the heart at the center of what is desired and perceived.

rightEvidence.title: Treasure locates the heart

compares.tension: Purity and treasure are not synonyms, and each saying supplies a distinct consequence.
compares.title: A heart that sees and a heart located by treasure

leftEvidence.role: The mountain and those called blessed
leftEvidence.title: Peacemakers will be called God’s children

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus calls peacemakers blessed.
points.right: Paul commands blessing persecutors, sharing joy and grief, humility, peace, and refusal of retaliation.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: They are promised recognition as children of God.
points.right: Vengeance is left to God, enemies receive food and drink, and evil is overcome with good.

compares.posture: Matthew names peacemakers; Romans develops peace, persecution, retaliation, and enemy care.

rightEvidence.title: Blessing persecutors and feeding enemies

compares.tension: Romans qualifies peace by “if possible,” while Matthew’s compact blessing does not discuss that limit.
compares.title: Making peace under hostility

leftEvidence.role: The mountain and those called blessed
leftEvidence.title: Persecution is joined to Kingdom and joy

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus calls people persecuted for righteousness and for his sake blessed.
points.right: Jesus recalls neighbor love and the saying to hate an enemy, then commands love, blessing, good, and prayer toward enemies and persecutors.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: He commands rejoicing because of heavenly reward and relates their treatment to earlier prophets.
points.right: The Father gives sun and rain to evil and good, and the hearers are called beyond reciprocal love toward perfection.

compares.posture: The blessing names hostility toward the hearers, and the later command directs their response toward hostile people.

rightEvidence.role: Law, righteousness, and the inner life
rightEvidence.title: Enemy love is grounded in the Father’s generosity

compares.tension: Being persecuted does not by itself prove righteousness; the sayings preserve “for righteousness” and “for my sake.”
compares.title: Persecuted people pray for persecutors

leftEvidence.role: The mountain and those called blessed
leftEvidence.title: Salt, light, and visible works

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus calls the hearers the earth’s salt and the world’s light, warning about salt that loses its function and light that is hidden.
points.right: Jesus warns against doing merciful deeds before people in order to be seen.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Their light is to shine so people see good works and glorify the Father.
points.right: Public reward is contrasted with hidden giving and the Father who sees in secret.

compares.posture: Good works are to be visible while merciful deeds are not to be performed for visibility.

rightEvidence.role: The Father who sees in secret
rightEvidence.title: Giving is tested by its audience

compares.tension: The difference turns on whom the action glorifies and why it is seen.
compares.title: Visible works and hidden practice

leftEvidence.role: Law, righteousness, and the inner life
leftEvidence.title: Jesus speaks of fulfilling law and prophets

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus denies coming to destroy the law or prophets and says he came to fulfill.
points.right: God speaks commandments concerning worship, name, Sabbath, family, murder, adultery, theft, witness, and desire.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Doing and teaching commandments are related to Kingdom standing, and entry requires righteousness beyond that of scribes and Pharisees.
points.right: The people fear the signs and ask Moses to mediate while he approaches the darkness.

compares.posture: Jesus names law and prophets before revisiting commands spoken at Sinai.

rightEvidence.title: God speaks commandments and the people stand back

compares.tension: Matthew’s fulfillment claim develops the commands without reproducing Sinai’s setting or whole speech.
compares.title: Commands spoken and fulfilled

leftEvidence.role: Law, righteousness, and the inner life
leftEvidence.title: Murder language reaches anger, speech, and reconciliation

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus recalls the murder command and extends danger of judgment to anger and contemptuous speech.
points.right: James contrasts human anger with God’s righteousness and calls hearers to receive the implanted word.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: A worshiper must seek reconciliation, and an adversary must be addressed before judgment closes the opportunity.
points.right: Hearing without doing is self-deception; continued doing, disciplined speech, care, and integrity characterize undefiled practice.

compares.posture: Matthew traces anger toward judgment and reconciliation; James says human anger does not produce God’s righteousness.

rightEvidence.title: Anger, hearing, doing, and the law of freedom

compares.tension: The sources share concern about anger but address different actions and community settings.
compares.title: Anger and righteousness

leftEvidence.role: Law, righteousness, and the inner life
leftEvidence.title: Adultery language reaches the desiring gaze

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus recalls the adultery command and locates adultery in a gaze directed toward lust.
points.right: God speaks commandments concerning worship, name, Sabbath, family, murder, adultery, theft, witness, and desire.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Severe eye-and-hand sayings frame the danger of stumbling and Gehenna.
points.right: The people fear the signs and ask Moses to mediate while he approaches the darkness.

compares.posture: Sinai forbids adultery and coveting; Matthew directs attention to a desiring gaze and the heart.

rightEvidence.title: God speaks commandments and the people stand back

compares.tension: The relation is intensifying and interpretive without declaring every desire identical to the completed act.
compares.title: Adultery, desire, and the heart

leftEvidence.role: Law, righteousness, and the inner life
leftEvidence.title: A divorce writing is set beside resulting adultery

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus recalls the requirement of a divorce writing and speaks about putting away a wife.
points.right: Jesus recalls the murder command and extends danger of judgment to anger and contemptuous speech.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: An exception is named, and later marriages are described through adultery language.
points.right: A worshiper must seek reconciliation, and an adversary must be addressed before judgment closes the opportunity.

compares.posture: Both sayings move from remembered legal instruction into present relational consequence.

rightEvidence.role: Law, righteousness, and the inner life
rightEvidence.title: Murder language reaches anger, speech, and reconciliation

compares.tension: Reconciliation is commanded in one case while the compressed divorce saying names no equivalent repair process.
compares.title: Broken relationship, legal action, and repair

leftEvidence.role: Law, righteousness, and the inner life
leftEvidence.title: Vows give way to unadorned yes and no

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus recalls commands about vows and says not to swear by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, or one’s head.
points.right: The LORD forbids theft, deception, false swearing, oppression, injustice, slander, hatred, vengeance, and grudges.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Speech is narrowed to a reliable yes or no.
points.right: The paragraph commands rebuke and love for one’s neighbor as oneself.

compares.posture: Leviticus forbids false swearing; Matthew rejects supporting ordinary truthfulness with invoked objects.

rightEvidence.title: Truth, judgment, inner hatred, and neighbor love stand together

compares.tension: Matthew’s broader instruction cannot be reduced to the Leviticus prohibition alone.
compares.title: False swearing and reliable speech

leftEvidence.role: Law, righteousness, and the inner life
leftEvidence.title: Measured retaliation gives way to costly nonresistance

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus recalls eye-for-eye language and answers injury, lawsuit, forced labor, requests, and borrowing with surprising actions.
points.right: Paul commands blessing persecutors, sharing joy and grief, humility, peace, and refusal of retaliation.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The hearer yields cheek, cloak, distance, gift, and access rather than matching harm.
points.right: Vengeance is left to God, enemies receive food and drink, and evil is overcome with good.

compares.posture: Matthew and Romans reject repaying harm with harm and turn toward costly good.

rightEvidence.title: Blessing persecutors and feeding enemies

compares.tension: Matthew uses compact cases; Romans explicitly leaves vengeance to God and qualifies peace by possibility.
compares.title: Refusing matched harm

leftEvidence.role: Law, righteousness, and the inner life
leftEvidence.title: Enemy love is grounded in the Father’s generosity

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus recalls neighbor love and the saying to hate an enemy, then commands love, blessing, good, and prayer toward enemies and persecutors.
points.right: Jesus commands love, good, blessing, prayer, nonretaliation, giving, and lending toward enemies.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The Father gives sun and rain to evil and good, and the hearers are called beyond reciprocal love toward perfection.
points.right: The Most High’s kindness to the unthankful and evil grounds the command to be merciful.

compares.posture: Both discourses ground enemy love in the Father’s generosity toward evil people.

rightEvidence.title: Luke ends enemy love with the Father’s mercy

compares.tension: Matthew concludes with perfection; Luke concludes with mercy, requiring source-language care.
compares.title: Perfect and merciful in enemy love

leftEvidence.role: The Father who sees in secret
leftEvidence.title: Giving is tested by its audience

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus warns against doing merciful deeds before people in order to be seen.
points.right: Jesus contrasts prayer for public notice with prayer behind a closed door and warns against vain repetition.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Public reward is contrasted with hidden giving and the Father who sees in secret.
points.right: The Father sees in secret and already knows what is needed before the request.

compares.posture: Both practices are tested by the difference between human notice and the Father who sees.

rightEvidence.role: The Father who sees in secret
rightEvidence.title: Prayer is separated from display and many words

compares.tension: Prayer adds the problem of many words and the Father’s prior knowledge.
compares.title: One hidden audience for giving and prayer

leftEvidence.role: The Father who sees in secret
leftEvidence.title: The disciples are given a shared prayer

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus teaches prayer addressed to “Our Father,” moving through God’s name, Kingdom, will, bread, debts, temptation, and evil.
points.right: After Jesus prays, a disciple asks to be taught, and Jesus gives a shorter prayer with sins and debts language.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The prayer is plural throughout and joins divine purposes to daily human need and responsibility.
points.right: A midnight-friend story and asking sayings lead to the Father giving the Holy Spirit.

compares.posture: Both prayers address the Father and ask for Kingdom, bread, forgiveness, and protection.

rightEvidence.title: A disciple’s request opens prayer and persistent asking

compares.tension: They differ in setting, length, debts and sins language, and the development that follows.
compares.title: Two prayers in two settings

leftEvidence.role: The Father who sees in secret
leftEvidence.title: Forgiving others is placed beside the Father’s forgiveness

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus states that forgiving people’s trespasses is followed by the Father’s forgiveness.
points.right: James prohibits partiality and says God chose the poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the Kingdom.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Refusing to forgive is followed by a negative statement about the Father’s forgiveness.
points.right: Neighbor love is called royal law, the whole law’s integrity is stressed, and mercy triumphs over judgment.

compares.posture: Both sources place human treatment of others beside a future divine response.

rightEvidence.title: The poor, Kingdom, neighbor love, and mercy meet judgment

compares.tension: Forgiveness and mercy overlap but remain distinct actions and arguments.
compares.title: Forgiveness, mercy, and reciprocal judgment

leftEvidence.role: The Father who sees in secret
leftEvidence.title: Fasting is hidden from the public gaze

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus warns against altering appearance so people notice a fast.
points.right: Jesus warns against doing merciful deeds before people in order to be seen.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Ordinary appearance hides the fast from people while the Father sees and rewards.
points.right: Public reward is contrasted with hidden giving and the Father who sees in secret.

compares.posture: Giving and fasting repeat the seen-by-people and seen-by-Father contrast.

rightEvidence.role: The Father who sees in secret
rightEvidence.title: Giving is tested by its audience

compares.tension: Their actions differ, and neither passage supplies a universal schedule for the practice.
compares.title: Hidden devotion and received reward

leftEvidence.role: Treasure, service, and tomorrow
leftEvidence.title: Treasure locates the heart

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus contrasts vulnerable earthly treasure with treasure in heaven.
points.right: Jesus tells disciples not to be anxious and directs them to ravens and lilies.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The heart is said to be where the treasure is.
points.right: The Father’s pleasure in giving the Kingdom leads to generosity, durable treasure, and the heart.

compares.posture: Matthew and Luke connect treasure location with the heart.

rightEvidence.title: Ravens, lilies, Kingdom, and treasure address fear

compares.tension: Luke explicitly joins the saying to generosity and the Father’s Kingdom gift.
compares.title: Treasure, generosity, and the heart

leftEvidence.role: Treasure, service, and tomorrow
leftEvidence.title: The eye fills the body with light or darkness

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus calls the eye the body’s lamp and contrasts a sound eye with an evil eye.
points.right: Jesus states that no one can serve two masters.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Whole-body light or darkness follows, ending with darkness mistaken for light.
points.right: Love and hate, devotion and contempt expose the division between God and Mammon.

compares.posture: The eye saying and two-master saying stand together between treasure and anxiety.

rightEvidence.title: God and Mammon cannot both be served

compares.tension: The discourse creates proximity without explicitly defining sound sight as service to God.
compares.title: Undivided sight and undivided service

leftEvidence.role: Treasure, service, and tomorrow
leftEvidence.title: God and Mammon cannot both be served

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus states that no one can serve two masters.
points.right: Jesus repeats the warning against anxious questions about necessities and contrasts the nations’ seeking with the Father’s knowledge.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Love and hate, devotion and contempt expose the division between God and Mammon.
points.right: The hearers are told to seek God’s Kingdom and righteousness first and to leave tomorrow’s trouble to tomorrow.

compares.posture: Exclusive service to God is followed by first seeking God’s Kingdom and righteousness.

rightEvidence.title: Kingdom seeking is placed before tomorrow

compares.tension: Seeking first does not answer every practical question about possession and provision.
compares.title: What is served and what is sought first

leftEvidence.role: Treasure, service, and tomorrow
leftEvidence.title: Life, birds, lilies, and little faith answer anxiety

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus says not to be anxious about food, drink, body, or clothing and directs attention to birds and lilies.
points.right: Jesus tells disciples not to be anxious and directs them to ravens and lilies.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The Father feeds and clothes; anxiety cannot add to life, and the hearers are called of little faith.
points.right: The Father’s pleasure in giving the Kingdom leads to generosity, durable treasure, and the heart.

compares.posture: Both settings use birds, lilies, value, and the Father to address anxiety.

rightEvidence.title: Ravens, lilies, Kingdom, and treasure address fear

compares.tension: Luke names ravens and little flock and moves into generosity; Matthew names tomorrow’s daily trouble.
compares.title: Birds, lilies, little faith, and the Father

leftEvidence.role: Treasure, service, and tomorrow
leftEvidence.title: Kingdom seeking is placed before tomorrow

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus repeats the warning against anxious questions about necessities and contrasts the nations’ seeking with the Father’s knowledge.
points.right: Jesus commands asking, seeking, and knocking and states that each receives a corresponding result.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The hearers are told to seek God’s Kingdom and righteousness first and to leave tomorrow’s trouble to tomorrow.
points.right: Human parents’ good gifts become the lesser case for the heavenly Father giving good things.

compares.posture: Kingdom seeking and asking sayings both direct desire toward the Father’s knowledge and goodness.

rightEvidence.title: Asking is grounded in the Father’s goodness

compares.tension: The texts do not promise that anxious desire or every requested object is simply granted as imagined.
compares.title: Seeking first and continuing to ask

leftEvidence.role: Judgment, discernment, and doing
leftEvidence.title: Judgment begins with the beam in one’s own eye

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus warns against judging because measure returns to the one who measures and contrasts another’s speck with one’s own beam.
points.right: Jesus links judging, condemning, releasing, and giving to reciprocal outcomes, then speaks of blind guides and beams.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Self-examination comes before helping remove another’s speck.
points.right: Teacher and disciple, tree and fruit, heart and speech complete the movement.

compares.posture: Matthew and Luke share judgment, measure, speck, and beam sayings.

rightEvidence.title: Judgment, measure, blindness, and fruit form one sequence

compares.tension: Luke surrounds them with condemnation, release, giving, blind guidance, training, fruit, and heart speech.
compares.title: Judging, measure, and the beam

leftEvidence.role: Judgment, discernment, and doing
leftEvidence.title: Holy things and pearls require discernment

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus warns against giving what is holy to dogs or throwing pearls before pigs.
points.right: Jesus warns about false prophets whose outward appearance hides predatory character.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Trampling and violent reversal are the named risks.
points.right: Good and corrupt trees are distinguished by fruit, and fruitless trees face fire.

compares.posture: Both sayings require attention to danger and outcome.

rightEvidence.title: False prophets are known by fruit

compares.tension: Dogs, pigs, false prophets, and fruit remain metaphors with different targets and evidence limits.
compares.title: Discernment after the warning against judgment

leftEvidence.role: Judgment, discernment, and doing
leftEvidence.title: Asking is grounded in the Father’s goodness

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus commands asking, seeking, and knocking and states that each receives a corresponding result.
points.right: After Jesus prays, a disciple asks to be taught, and Jesus gives a shorter prayer with sins and debts language.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Human parents’ good gifts become the lesser case for the heavenly Father giving good things.
points.right: A midnight-friend story and asking sayings lead to the Father giving the Holy Spirit.

compares.posture: Matthew and Luke share asking, seeking, knocking, human-parent comparison, and the Father’s gift.

rightEvidence.title: A disciple’s request opens prayer and persistent asking

compares.tension: Matthew names good things; Luke names the Holy Spirit and precedes the sayings with persistence.
compares.title: Asking in two settings

leftEvidence.role: Judgment, discernment, and doing
leftEvidence.title: The law and prophets are gathered into reciprocal action

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus tells hearers to do to others what they desire others to do to them.
points.right: The LORD forbids theft, deception, false swearing, oppression, injustice, slander, hatred, vengeance, and grudges.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: He calls this the law and the prophets.
points.right: The paragraph commands rebuke and love for one’s neighbor as oneself.

compares.posture: Matthew’s reciprocal action and Leviticus’s neighbor-love command both summarize relational responsibility.

rightEvidence.title: Truth, judgment, inner hatred, and neighbor love stand together

compares.tension: Matthew calls its saying law and prophets without repeating Leviticus’s full social context.
compares.title: Doing to others and loving the neighbor

leftEvidence.role: Judgment, discernment, and doing
leftEvidence.title: Two gates lead toward destruction and life

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus commands entry through the narrow gate and contrasts broad and restricted ways.
points.right: The psalm calls one person blessed for rejecting wicked counsel and delighting in the LORD’s law.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Many enter the way to destruction; few find the way to life.
points.right: Fruitful tree and driven chaff images end in known and perishing ways.

compares.posture: Both sources contrast paths through life, judgment, and destruction.

rightEvidence.title: Blessing opens into two ways and two outcomes

compares.tension: Matthew emphasizes entry and finding; the psalm emphasizes counsel, law, fruit, and God’s knowledge of the way.
compares.title: Two ways and their outcomes

leftEvidence.role: Judgment, discernment, and doing
leftEvidence.title: False prophets are known by fruit

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus warns about false prophets whose outward appearance hides predatory character.
points.right: James contrasts human anger with God’s righteousness and calls hearers to receive the implanted word.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Good and corrupt trees are distinguished by fruit, and fruitless trees face fire.
points.right: Hearing without doing is self-deception; continued doing, disciplined speech, care, and integrity characterize undefiled practice.

compares.posture: Matthew tests prophets by fruit; James tests hearing by doing and lived practice.

rightEvidence.title: Anger, hearing, doing, and the law of freedom

compares.tension: Fruit and doing are related evidence categories without being identical measures.
compares.title: Fruit, hearing, and embodied practice

leftEvidence.role: Judgment, discernment, and doing
leftEvidence.title: Speaking and mighty works do not replace being known

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus says not everyone calling him Lord enters the Kingdom, but the one doing his Father’s will does.
points.right: Jesus compares everyone hearing and doing his words to a wise builder on rock.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Claims of prophecy, exorcism, and mighty works meet the reply, “I never knew you.”
points.right: The same storm exposes the difference between a house that stands and one that falls.

compares.posture: Both closing sayings contrast verbal proximity to Jesus with action.

rightEvidence.title: Hearing and doing determine the foundation

compares.tension: Mighty works and a storm-tested foundation expose different ways that appearance can fail.
compares.title: Saying Lord and doing the words

leftEvidence.role: Judgment, discernment, and doing
leftEvidence.title: Hearing and doing determine the foundation

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Jesus compares everyone hearing and doing his words to a wise builder on rock.
points.right: Jesus asks why people call him Lord without doing what he says.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The same storm exposes the difference between a house that stands and one that falls.
points.right: One builder digs deep to rock; the other builds without a foundation, and the stream exposes both.

compares.posture: Both versions make hearing and doing decisive under destructive pressure.

rightEvidence.title: Luke’s builders dig deep or lack a foundation

compares.tension: Matthew contrasts rock and sand with rain, floods, and winds; Luke contrasts deep foundation with no foundation and a stream.
compares.title: Two versions of the builders

leftEvidence.role: Judgment, discernment, and doing
leftEvidence.title: The crowds respond to Jesus’ authority

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Matthew reports that Jesus finishes the sayings and the crowds are astonished.
points.right: Jesus comes down from the mountain with crowds following, and a leper asks to be cleansed if Jesus wills.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: They distinguish his teaching authority from that of their scribes.
points.right: Jesus touches and cleanses him, then directs him to the priest and Moses’ commanded gift.

compares.posture: Crowds respond to Jesus’ teaching, then follow as a leper approaches Jesus’ will and power.

rightEvidence.title: Jesus descends and a leper approaches

compares.tension: Astonishment is not the same response as the leper’s appeal and obedience.
compares.title: Authority heard and authority encountered

leftEvidence.role: The mountain and those called blessed
leftEvidence.title: Jesus sits and begins to teach

points.label: Event action and claim
points.left: Seeing the crowds, Jesus goes up the mountain, sits, and receives his disciples.
points.right: Thunder, cloud, trumpet, fire, and shaking accompany the LORD’s descent on Sinai and Moses’ ascent.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: He opens his mouth and teaches them.
points.right: The people remain below guarded boundaries while God answers Moses by voice.

compares.posture: Both scenes gather people around a mountain and authoritative speech.

rightEvidence.title: A mountain, gathered people, and a voice at Sinai

compares.tension: Sinai guards distance around Moses’ ascent; Matthew seats Jesus with disciples approaching him.
compares.title: Two mountain instruction settings

edges.basis: The antecedent explains the large following; the opening narrows attention to disciples around the seated teacher. The discourse’s immediate and wider audiences remain visible without an invented movement.
edges.label: Crowds gather and disciples draw near

edges.basis: Matthew and Luke open corresponding blessing sequences with materially different wording. Matthew adds “in spirit”; Luke directly addresses the poor and later speaks woes to the rich.
edges.label: Poor in spirit and poor

edges.basis: Both sayings hold present grief beside a promised reversal. Matthew says mourners will be comforted; Luke says present weepers will laugh and follows with a woe to those laughing now.
edges.label: Mourning, weeping, comfort, and laughter

edges.basis: Matthew’s inheritance wording and Psalm 1’s two ways place present character beside future outcome. The promised earth and the known way are related outcomes, not identical images.
edges.label: The gentle inherit and the righteous way endures

edges.basis: Both blessings promise filling to the hungry. Matthew names righteousness as hunger’s object; Luke addresses those hungry now and gives a corresponding woe to the full.
edges.label: Hunger for righteousness and hunger now

edges.basis: Matthew’s reciprocal blessing and James’s judgment saying make mercy consequential. Neither source reduces mercy to sentiment, while their arguments and audiences differ.
edges.label: Mercy received and mercy at judgment

edges.basis: Both sayings place the heart at the center of what is desired and perceived. Purity and treasure are not synonyms, and each saying supplies a distinct consequence.
edges.label: A heart that sees and a heart located by treasure

edges.basis: Matthew names peacemakers; Romans develops peace, persecution, retaliation, and enemy care. Romans qualifies peace by “if possible,” while Matthew’s compact blessing does not discuss that limit.
edges.label: Making peace under hostility

edges.basis: The blessing names hostility toward the hearers, and the later command directs their response toward hostile people. Being persecuted does not by itself prove righteousness; the sayings preserve “for righteousness” and “for my sake.”
edges.label: Persecuted people pray for persecutors

edges.basis: Good works are to be visible while merciful deeds are not to be performed for visibility. The difference turns on whom the action glorifies and why it is seen.
edges.label: Visible works and hidden practice

edges.basis: Jesus names law and prophets before revisiting commands spoken at Sinai. Matthew’s fulfillment claim develops the commands without reproducing Sinai’s setting or whole speech.
edges.label: Commands spoken and fulfilled

edges.basis: Matthew traces anger toward judgment and reconciliation; James says human anger does not produce God’s righteousness. The sources share concern about anger but address different actions and community settings.
edges.label: Anger and righteousness

edges.basis: Sinai forbids adultery and coveting; Matthew directs attention to a desiring gaze and the heart. The relation is intensifying and interpretive without declaring every desire identical to the completed act.
edges.label: Adultery, desire, and the heart

edges.basis: Both sayings move from remembered legal instruction into present relational consequence. Reconciliation is commanded in one case while the compressed divorce saying names no equivalent repair process.
edges.label: Broken relationship, legal action, and repair

edges.basis: Leviticus forbids false swearing; Matthew rejects supporting ordinary truthfulness with invoked objects. Matthew’s broader instruction cannot be reduced to the Leviticus prohibition alone.
edges.label: False swearing and reliable speech

edges.basis: Matthew and Romans reject repaying harm with harm and turn toward costly good. Matthew uses compact cases; Romans explicitly leaves vengeance to God and qualifies peace by possibility.
edges.label: Refusing matched harm

edges.basis: Both discourses ground enemy love in the Father’s generosity toward evil people. Matthew concludes with perfection; Luke concludes with mercy, requiring source-language care.
edges.label: Perfect and merciful in enemy love

edges.basis: Both practices are tested by the difference between human notice and the Father who sees. Prayer adds the problem of many words and the Father’s prior knowledge.
edges.label: One hidden audience for giving and prayer

edges.basis: Both prayers address the Father and ask for Kingdom, bread, forgiveness, and protection. They differ in setting, length, debts and sins language, and the development that follows.
edges.label: Two prayers in two settings

edges.basis: Both sources place human treatment of others beside a future divine response. Forgiveness and mercy overlap but remain distinct actions and arguments.
edges.label: Forgiveness, mercy, and reciprocal judgment

edges.basis: Giving and fasting repeat the seen-by-people and seen-by-Father contrast. Their actions differ, and neither passage supplies a universal schedule for the practice.
edges.label: Hidden devotion and received reward

edges.basis: Matthew and Luke connect treasure location with the heart. Luke explicitly joins the saying to generosity and the Father’s Kingdom gift.
edges.label: Treasure, generosity, and the heart

edges.basis: The eye saying and two-master saying stand together between treasure and anxiety. The discourse creates proximity without explicitly defining sound sight as service to God.
edges.label: Undivided sight and undivided service

edges.basis: Exclusive service to God is followed by first seeking God’s Kingdom and righteousness. Seeking first does not answer every practical question about possession and provision.
edges.label: What is served and what is sought first

edges.basis: Both settings use birds, lilies, value, and the Father to address anxiety. Luke names ravens and little flock and moves into generosity; Matthew names tomorrow’s daily trouble.
edges.label: Birds, lilies, little faith, and the Father

edges.basis: Kingdom seeking and asking sayings both direct desire toward the Father’s knowledge and goodness. The texts do not promise that anxious desire or every requested object is simply granted as imagined.
edges.label: Seeking first and continuing to ask

edges.basis: Matthew and Luke share judgment, measure, speck, and beam sayings. Luke surrounds them with condemnation, release, giving, blind guidance, training, fruit, and heart speech.
edges.label: Judging, measure, and the beam

edges.basis: Both sayings require attention to danger and outcome. Dogs, pigs, false prophets, and fruit remain metaphors with different targets and evidence limits.
edges.label: Discernment after the warning against judgment

edges.basis: Matthew and Luke share asking, seeking, knocking, human-parent comparison, and the Father’s gift. Matthew names good things; Luke names the Holy Spirit and precedes the sayings with persistence.
edges.label: Asking in two settings

edges.basis: Matthew’s reciprocal action and Leviticus’s neighbor-love command both summarize relational responsibility. Matthew calls its saying law and prophets without repeating Leviticus’s full social context.
edges.label: Doing to others and loving the neighbor

edges.basis: Both sources contrast paths through life, judgment, and destruction. Matthew emphasizes entry and finding; the psalm emphasizes counsel, law, fruit, and God’s knowledge of the way.
edges.label: Two ways and their outcomes

edges.basis: Matthew tests prophets by fruit; James tests hearing by doing and lived practice. Fruit and doing are related evidence categories without being identical measures.
edges.label: Fruit, hearing, and embodied practice

edges.basis: Both closing sayings contrast verbal proximity to Jesus with action. Mighty works and a storm-tested foundation expose different ways that appearance can fail.
edges.label: Saying Lord and doing the words

edges.basis: Both versions make hearing and doing decisive under destructive pressure. Matthew contrasts rock and sand with rain, floods, and winds; Luke contrasts deep foundation with no foundation and a stream.
edges.label: Two versions of the builders

edges.basis: Crowds respond to Jesus’ teaching, then follow as a leper approaches Jesus’ will and power. Astonishment is not the same response as the leper’s appeal and obedience.
edges.label: Authority heard and authority encountered

edges.basis: Both scenes gather people around a mountain and authoritative speech. Sinai guards distance around Moses’ ascent; Matthew seats Jesus with disciples approaching him.
edges.label: Two mountain instruction settings

event.centerRule: Matthew’s complete mountain discourse remains the Event center. Related texts enter only when they materially prepare, parallel, contrast, clarify, or reuse its language, and every source keeps its own setting and wording.

Fruitful tree and driven chaff images end in known and perishing ways.
blessed · law · tree · fruit · judgment · way · perish
The psalm remains its own poem and does not supply a one-to-one key for every sermon image.

passages.contextLine: Earlier words and later echoes · Romans 12:14–21

dimensions.label: Paul commands blessing persecutors, sharing joy and grief, humility, peace, and refusal of retaliation.
Vengeance is left to God, enemies receive food and drink, and evil is overcome with good.
bless persecutors · repay no evil · peace · vengeance · feed enemy · overcome evil
Romans does not explicitly cite the Sermon on the Mount as its source.

passages.contextLine: Earlier words and later echoes · James 1:19–27

dimensions.label: James contrasts human anger with God’s righteousness and calls hearers to receive the implanted word.
Hearing without doing is self-deception; continued doing, disciplined speech, care, and integrity characterize undefiled practice.
slow to anger · righteousness · hearer · doer · law of freedom · blessed
The passage does not identify itself as a commentary on Matthew’s discourse.

dimensions.label: James prohibits partiality and says God chose the poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the Kingdom.
Neighbor love is called royal law, the whole law’s integrity is stressed, and mercy triumphs over judgment.
poor · rich in faith · heirs of Kingdom · neighbor · law · mercy · judgment
The overlap supports comparison without proving that every phrase depends directly on Matthew.

pivots.description: Crowds gather, Jesus sits with disciples, and the opening blessings name people whose present condition and promised future do not look alike.

nodes.note: Jesus teaches in Galilee, announces the Kingdom, heals disease, and becomes known across a wide region.
nodes.title: Teaching, healing, and crowds gather before the mountain

nodes.note: Seeing the crowds, Jesus goes up the mountain, sits, and receives his disciples.
nodes.title: Jesus sits and begins to teach

nodes.note: Jesus calls the poor in spirit blessed.
nodes.title: The poor in spirit receive the Kingdom

nodes.note: Jesus calls those who mourn blessed.
nodes.title: Those who mourn will be comforted

nodes.note: Jesus calls the gentle blessed.
nodes.title: The gentle will inherit the earth

nodes.note: Jesus calls those who hunger and thirst for righteousness blessed.
nodes.title: Hunger for righteousness will be filled

nodes.note: Jesus calls the merciful blessed.
nodes.title: The merciful will receive mercy

nodes.note: Jesus calls the pure in heart blessed.
nodes.title: The pure in heart will see God

nodes.note: Jesus calls peacemakers blessed.
nodes.title: Peacemakers will be called God’s children

nodes.note: Jesus calls people persecuted for righteousness and for his sake blessed.
nodes.title: Persecution is joined to Kingdom and joy

nodes.note: Jesus calls the hearers the earth’s salt and the world’s light, warning about salt that loses its function and light that is hidden.
nodes.title: Salt, light, and visible works

pivots.title: The mountain and those called blessed

pivots.description: Jesus denies abolishing the law and prophets, then carries murder, adultery, divorce, vows, retaliation, and neighbor love into speech, desire, action, and relationship.

nodes.note: Jesus denies coming to destroy the law or prophets and says he came to fulfill.
nodes.title: Jesus speaks of fulfilling law and prophets

nodes.note: Jesus recalls the murder command and extends danger of judgment to anger and contemptuous speech.
nodes.title: Murder language reaches anger, speech, and reconciliation

nodes.note: Jesus recalls the adultery command and locates adultery in a gaze directed toward lust.
nodes.title: Adultery language reaches the desiring gaze

nodes.note: Jesus recalls the requirement of a divorce writing and speaks about putting away a wife.
nodes.title: A divorce writing is set beside resulting adultery

nodes.note: Jesus recalls commands about vows and says not to swear by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, or one’s head.
nodes.title: Vows give way to unadorned yes and no

nodes.note: Jesus recalls eye-for-eye language and answers injury, lawsuit, forced labor, requests, and borrowing with surprising actions.
nodes.title: Measured retaliation gives way to costly nonresistance

nodes.note: Jesus recalls neighbor love and the saying to hate an enemy, then commands love, blessing, good, and prayer toward enemies and persecutors.
nodes.title: Enemy love is grounded in the Father’s generosity

pivots.title: Law, righteousness, and the inner life

pivots.description: Giving, prayer, forgiveness, and fasting are inspected through audience, motive, hidden practice, and the Father who knows and sees.

nodes.note: Jesus warns against doing merciful deeds before people in order to be seen.
nodes.title: Giving is tested by its audience

nodes.note: Jesus contrasts prayer for public notice with prayer behind a closed door and warns against vain repetition.
nodes.title: Prayer is separated from display and many words

nodes.note: Jesus teaches prayer addressed to “Our Father,” moving through God’s name, Kingdom, will, bread, debts, temptation, and evil.
nodes.title: The disciples are given a shared prayer

nodes.note: Jesus states that forgiving people’s trespasses is followed by the Father’s forgiveness.
nodes.title: Forgiving others is placed beside the Father’s forgiveness

nodes.note: Jesus warns against altering appearance so people notice a fast.
nodes.title: Fasting is hidden from the public gaze

pivots.title: The Father who sees in secret

pivots.description: Treasure and sight lead into divided service, daily provision, anxiety, value, Kingdom seeking, and the limit of tomorrow.

nodes.note: Jesus contrasts vulnerable earthly treasure with treasure in heaven.
nodes.title: Treasure locates the heart

nodes.note: Jesus calls the eye the body’s lamp and contrasts a sound eye with an evil eye.
nodes.title: The eye fills the body with light or darkness

nodes.note: Jesus states that no one can serve two masters.
nodes.title: God and Mammon cannot both be served

nodes.note: Jesus says not to be anxious about food, drink, body, or clothing and directs attention to birds and lilies.
nodes.title: Life, birds, lilies, and little faith answer anxiety

nodes.note: Jesus repeats the warning against anxious questions about necessities and contrasts the nations’ seeking with the Father’s knowledge.
nodes.title: Kingdom seeking is placed before tomorrow

pivots.title: Treasure, service, and tomorrow

pivots.description: The discourse closes through judgment, discernment, asking, two ways, fruit, profession, obedience, foundations, and the crowd’s response to authority.

nodes.note: Jesus warns against judging because measure returns to the one who measures and contrasts another’s speck with one’s own beam.
nodes.title: Judgment begins with the beam in one’s own eye

nodes.note: Jesus warns against giving what is holy to dogs or throwing pearls before pigs.
nodes.title: Holy things and pearls require discernment

nodes.note: Jesus commands asking, seeking, and knocking and states that each receives a corresponding result.
nodes.title: Asking is grounded in the Father’s goodness

nodes.note: Jesus tells hearers to do to others what they desire others to do to them.
nodes.title: The law and prophets are gathered into reciprocal action

nodes.note: Jesus commands entry through the narrow gate and contrasts broad and restricted ways.
nodes.title: Two gates lead toward destruction and life

nodes.note: Jesus warns about false prophets whose outward appearance hides predatory character.
nodes.title: False prophets are known by fruit

nodes.note: Jesus says not everyone calling him Lord enters the Kingdom, but the one doing his Father’s will does.
nodes.title: Speaking and mighty works do not replace being known

nodes.note: Jesus compares everyone hearing and doing his words to a wise builder on rock.
nodes.title: Hearing and doing determine the foundation

nodes.note: Matthew reports that Jesus finishes the sayings and the crowds are astonished.
nodes.title: The crowds respond to Jesus’ authority

nodes.note: Jesus comes down from the mountain with crowds following, and a leper asks to be cleansed if Jesus wills.
nodes.title: Jesus descends and a leper approaches

pivots.title: Judgment, discernment, and doing

nodes.note: Jesus stands on a level place among disciples and a crowd, heals, and addresses the poor, hungry, weeping, and rejected.
nodes.title: Luke places blessings and woes on a level place

nodes.note: Jesus commands love, good, blessing, prayer, nonretaliation, giving, and lending toward enemies.
nodes.title: Luke ends enemy love with the Father’s mercy

nodes.note: Jesus links judging, condemning, releasing, and giving to reciprocal outcomes, then speaks of blind guides and beams.
nodes.title: Judgment, measure, blindness, and fruit form one sequence

nodes.note: Jesus asks why people call him Lord without doing what he says.
nodes.title: Luke’s builders dig deep or lack a foundation

nodes.note: After Jesus prays, a disciple asks to be taught, and Jesus gives a shorter prayer with sins and debts language.
nodes.title: A disciple’s request opens prayer and persistent asking

nodes.note: Jesus tells disciples not to be anxious and directs them to ravens and lilies.
nodes.title: Ravens, lilies, Kingdom, and treasure address fear
